title: Multi-Task Framework for Efficient Knee Osteoarthritis Segmentation and Classification
abstract: Abstract Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of chronic disability worldwide, and magnetic reso- nance imaging (MRI) remains the gold standard for assessing cartilage and meniscal integrity. While 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can leverage volumetric context for KOA analysis, they often incur high computational cost, increased memory demands, and susceptibility to learning from anatomically irrelevant regions. In this work, we propose a unified and flexible multi-task learning framework that accommodates both 2D slice-based and 3D volume-based convolutional backbones for joint KOA classification and knee structure segmentation. The architecture integrates a shared encoder configurable as either 2D or 3D followed by two task-specific branches: a dual-headed segmentation decoder for meniscus and cartilage masks, and a classification head operating on globally pooled features for KOA detection. We train and validate the framework on a large-scale dataset of 105,919 MRI slices, including expert-annotated segmentation masks and radiographically verified KOA labels. The multi-task design enables concurrent learning of anatomical and diagnostic signals at either the slice or volume level, improving task synergy and anatomical focus. Comparative evaluations demonstrate that the 2D variant achieves more consistent segmentation quality, faster convergence, and lower computational overhead than a 3D VGG-UNet baseline while also delivering improved KOA classification accuracy.

title: Staged Management of Recurrent Obstructed Hemivagina in Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich Syndrome: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Background Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome (HWWS) is a rare congenital Müllerian anomaly characterized by uterus didelphys, obstructed hemivagina, and ipsilateral renal anomaly. Recurrence after prior surgical treatment is particularly rare. We report a complex recurrent case of obstructed hemivagina in a patient with HWWS and duplicated vagina, successfully managed with a staged surgical approach. Case presentation A 19-year-old woman with a history of two prior vaginal septum resections and excision of a perineal mass (histopathology confirming ectopic colonic tissue) presented with recurrent pelvic pain and fever. MRI and endoscopic assessment demonstrated uterus didelphys, duplicated cervices and vaginas, complete obstruction of the right hemivagina, ipsilateral renal agenesis, and a deeply recessed obstructed cavity containing purulent fluid. Because of the markedly distorted postoperative anatomy, a staged surgical strategy was adopted. The first stage involved hysteroscopic and vaginoscopic decompression with ultrasound-guided septal incision and drainage. The second stage consisted of definitive reconstruction, including resection of the accessory blind tract, obliteration of the residual obstructed cavity, and perineal reconstruction. The patient recovered uneventfully, resumed regular painless menstruation. No recurrence of hemivaginal obstruction was observed during follow-up.However, the diagnosis was not definitive. The patient had lifelong persistent urinary incontinence that showed no improvement after surgery. Although a right ectopic ureter or ureterocele was unlikely to account for the continuous leakage because the right kidney was nonfunctioning, a left ectopic ureter and other lower urinary tract abnormalities had not been fully excluded. Conclusions This case highlights a complex recurrent presentation of HWWS and emphasizes the importance of MRI and endoscopic evaluation in delineating atypical postoperative anatomy. Individualized staged surgical management may help prevent re-obstruction, control infection, restore functional genital tract continuity, and preserve future reproductive potential in patients with complicated or recurrent HWWS. Persistent urinary incontinence and a history of perineal ectopic colonic tissue warrant further urological and multidisciplinary evaluation, a left ectopic ureter and other lower urinary tract abnormalities should be carefully evaluated in this patients.

title: Quality Assessment and Model Training Impact of Synthetic Images in Medical Diagnostic Imaging: Systematic Review.
abstract: Background AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network-based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of -10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), F 1 -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. For researchers, developers, and regulators, these findings highlight the need for standardized multimethod image-quality evaluation, complete reporting, and rigorous external validation before synthetic-image pipelines are translated into clinical AI applications.

title: Multimodal Visual Question Answering System for Survival Prognosis in PSMA-Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
abstract: Large language models show great promise for clinical decision support but generally lack medical imaging integration. Therefore, vision-language models have been proposed, but there is little evidence on their performance, particularly compared with conventional machine learning. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is a well-established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but it is still not known which patients will be good long-term responders. Therefore, this study proposes a physician-inspired visual question answering (VQA) framework that emulates the structured integration of PSMA-directed imaging and clinical data used in routine clinical assessment for overall survival prognostication. Methods: As a proof of concept, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter study across 2 academic institutions that included 110 patients with mCRPC who were treated with either [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T or [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Our VQA approach incorporates a 3-dimensional image encoder, the domain-specific language model RadBERT, and a cross-modal transformer to process baseline and interim (after 2 cycles) PET and SPECT images, clinical data, and clinical query. The model was trained to predict 24-mo survival, and performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. External validation was performed with the [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 cohort. Results: The VQA model outperformed all state-of-the-art approaches while showing accuracy comparable to the query-free attention multimodal fusion model. Specifically, it achieved 81.8% accuracy (95% CI, 0.52-0.95) when integrating SPECT or PET images with prostate-specific antigen measurements. External validation of the VQA showed 71.9% accuracy (95% CI, 0.53-0.86) after few-shot fine-tuning, with further improvement over all state-of-the-art approaches in survival stratification. The VQA approach showed the closest calibration with the ground-truth survival distribution, with no significant differences observed (log-rank test, P = 0.76). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed the highest area under the curve (0.75) among the evaluated models. Together, these findings suggest that the VQA approach demonstrated adaptability across different PSMA ligands while maintaining slightly improved yet comparable overall survival prognostic performance. Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

title: Radiopharmaceutical Therapy with [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in Refractory Meningiomas: Results from the French Multicenter MELUTE Cohort.
abstract: Evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas derives mainly from small, single-center studies. The French national multicenter MELUTE study aimed to consolidate these data using a standardized regimen within a compassionate-use program approved by a national multidisciplinary tumor board. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, patients with refractory meningiomas treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in 18 French centers between July 2022 and December 2024 were included. Treatment consisted of 7.4 GBq every 8 wk for up to 4 cycles. Clinical data (demographics, histologic World Health Organization grade [WHO], prior treatments, number of cycles, toxicity, progression, survival status as of October 1, 2025) were collected. Baseline [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTATOC PET and brain MRI scans obtained before and after treatment were centrally reviewed. The primary endpoint was 6-mo progression-free survival (PFS) assessed using volumetric Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Group criteria. Secondary endpoints were PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Sixty-nine patients were included (mean age, 65.1 ± 13.2 y; 52% female): 13 WHO grade 1, 42 WHO grade 2, 8 WHO grade 3, and 6 without histology. Most had prior surgery (86%) or radiotherapy (93%); 32% received prior systemic therapy. Twelve patients (17%) did not complete 4 cycles; only one discontinuation was toxicity-related. Six-month PFS was 70% (95% CI, 58.7-80.4%). Median PFS was 14.6 mo (95% CI, 13.3-18.5 mo), and median OS was 27.6 mo (95% CI, 24.2 mo to not reached). Grade 3 adverse events, mainly lymphopenia, occurred in 16%. Meningioma WHO grade independently predicted PFS, whereas higher Karnofsky performance status and corticosteroid use were protective; worse OS was associated with higher baseline tumor growth rate and prior systemic therapy. Conclusion: MELUTE demonstrates promising efficacy and favorable safety of [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas with limited therapeutic options.

title: Test-Retest Repeatability of [<sup>18</sup>F]FDG Uptake by Solid Tumors on PET/MRI: A Prospective, Multicenter Study Using the QIBA Protocol.
abstract: Prior oncologic PET/MRI repeatability studies have been limited by single-center designs, small cohorts, or select patient populations. Our primary aim was to estimate the test-retest repeatability of uptake metrics on [ 18 F]FDG PET/MRI studies across a variety of cancer types. A secondary aim was to assess the impact of intersession μ-map variability on repeatability. Methods: In this prospective study involving 2 institutions with different PET/MRI scanners, subjects completing standard-of-care [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT or MRI examinations were recruited to undergo 2 research [ 18 F]FDG PET/MRIs (i.e., test and retest) within a 1-9 d period per Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance specifications. Intersession μ-map variations had minimal negative impact on repeatability.

title: B7H3-Targeted Molecular Imaging for Highly Specific Diagnosis and In Vivo Noninvasive Detection of B7H3 in Breast Cancer.
abstract: B7 homolog 3 (B7H3) is widely expressed in solid tumors, but its role in the diagnosis of breast cancer is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT in breast cancer patients. Methods: Thirty patients with diverse subtypes of breast cancer underwent both [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH and [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. Immunohistochemical staining for B7H3 was performed in 25 patients. Results: B7H3 positivity was detected in 84% of samples by immunohistochemistry. [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH demonstrated a higher lesion detection rate compared with [ 18 F]FDG (96.8% vs. 92.4%) among 157 lesions. Median SUV max was 9.5 in strongly positive lesions; bone metastases had the highest uptake (median SUV max , 10.9). Imaging resulted in changing the stage or treatment in 8 patients. Hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative lesions showed the highest B7H3 positivity (87.5%) and uptake (median SUV max , 10.5). Conclusion: [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT offers high sensitivity for staging advanced breast cancer and noninvasive B7H3 screening. It may influence clinical decisions and appears to reveal subtype-specific uptake, with a tendency to favor hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative disease.

title: Novel Neuroimaging Biomarker of Cortical Gray/White Border Integrity in Blast-Related Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Background and purpose Recent studies suggest that blast or mid-impact neurotrauma are characterized by scar-border forming astrogliosis at the gray-white matter junction. Individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and blast trauma have increased neuroinflammation and impairment of axonal remyelination on postmortem histopathology. However, there are currently only limited methodologies to use in the assessment of the cortical gray/white interface using in vivo neuroimaging. The purpose was to investigate the gray-white matter contrast (GWC) at the gray-white matter junction that may be linked to neuroinflammation/astrogliosis in the setting of blast exposure and/or mTBI, through 3D T1-weighted MPRAGE images. Materials and methods Post-9/11 veterans ( n =723) from the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders completed MRI. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: participants with a history of blast-related mTBI (blast-mTBI), participants with a history of mTBI due to other mechanical forces (blunt-mTBI), participants with a history of close blast exposure but no mTBI, and those without a history of lifetime mTBI or close blast exposure. MRI data processing for morphometry and cortical surface mapping was done using FreeSurfer image analysis. Signal intensities in gray and white matter along the cortical and white matter interface were used to calculate mean GWC value. Results Veterans in the blast-mTBI group showed diffuse patterns of increased GWC relative to the other groups, particularly in the frontotemporal lobes. This effect was driven primarily by a greater number of high GWC regions in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma and blunt-mTBI groups. Conclusions There was diffuse increased GWC on MR in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma, close blast exposure, and blunt-mTBI groups. These findings may be linked to astrogliosis and neuroinflammation in patients with blast-mTBI. Histopathologic correlation with imaging findings will be necessary to better understand these effects.

title: Clinical Presentation, Misdiagnosis, and Imaging Findings of Anterior Disc Herniations.
abstract: Anterior and anterolateral lumbar disc herniations are uncommon and usually do not present with classic radicular symptoms. This contributes to a broader and sometimes misleading differential diagnosis based on the initial presentation. When identified on cross-sectional imaging performed for nonspinal indications, displaced disc material can be mistaken for a retroperitoneal mass, potentially prompting additional imaging or invasive evaluation. We report 6 cases of anterior and anterolateral disc herniations identified on CT and MRI, including some patients presenting with abdominal or flank pain. Imaging demonstrated anterior disc extrusion, some with marked inflammatory changes. In some cases, the initial diagnosis included retroperitoneal neoplasm or an inflammatory process. Recognizing this imaging pattern and its clinical context may help accurate diagnosis, avoid unnecessary procedures, and guide appropriate management.

title: The reliability of clinical judgments in dermatology: a descriptive review on their role as a reference standard for technological diagnostic research.
abstract: The expansion of dermatological mobile health (mHealth) and teledermatology has generated numerous diagnostic support tools, typically validated against traditional face-to-face assessments. Histopathological confirmation through skin biopsy is invasive, resource-intensive and, in many African settings, not readily available as a dermatological research reference standard. Yet, the reliability of clinical diagnoses used as such standards remains uncertain. The study objective was to assess the consistency (inter-rater reliability) of face-to-face clinical judgments among multiple dermatologists evaluating the same patient group. For this descriptive literature review, a comprehensive search of seven databases and information platforms was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) reporting guideline. In total, 1,700 studies were found after deduplication and screened using pre-set criteria. Eighteen studies were included: three compared clinical diagnoses directly and 15 assessed the reliability of dermatological scoring systems for disease severity and activity. All studies involved two or more dermatologists assessing the same patients. Reported agreement among raters ranged from 0.15 to 0.98 for studies evaluating clinical diagnosis and from 0.07 to 0.95 for studies assessing disease severity or activity scores, demonstrating wide variability in inter-rater reliability. In conclusion, clinical diagnosis alone, especially if made by one or a limited number of dermatologists, may not provide a sufficiently reliable reference standard for validating teledermatology, dermatological mHealth applications, or artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Strengthening evidence on the reliability of diagnostic reference standards is essential for evaluating emerging digital health innovations, particularly in regions with limited access to dermatologists and histopathology services. Future studies, with similarly experienced dermatological assessors, should have larger sample sizes, assess diagnostic agreement rather than disease severity outcomes, combine inter- and intra-rater assessments, and include diverse geographic contexts such as Africa, Asia and Latin America. The potential influence of assessors' levels of experience on agreement should also be explored. A final recommendation is to come to a consensus about skin color classification.

title: Completion cholecystectomy for remnant gall bladder stones: A tertiary centre experience.
abstract: Introduction Remnant gall bladder and cystic duct stump calculi are uncommon but significant causes of post-cholecystectomy syndrome, often presenting after a prolonged interval and posing diagnostic and technical challenges. Evidence from contemporary Indian cohorts remains limited and heterogeneous. Patients and methods This retrospective observational study analysed 22 consecutive patients who underwent completion cholecystectomy for symptomatic remnant gall bladder or cystic duct stump calculi between January 2015 and December 2024 at a tertiary referral centre. Patients with radiologically confirmed remnant pathology and prior sub-total or difficult cholecystectomy were included. Clinical, imaging, operative, perioperative and follow-up outcomes were analysed. Results The mean age was 47.8 years with female predominance (77.2%). The median interval between index surgery and symptom onset was 4 years. Biliary colic was the most common presentation (86.4%), with complications in 18.2% of patients. Ultrasonography detected pathology in 76%, whereas magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) demonstrated 100% diagnostic accuracy. title: Atropine-Associated Central Anticholinergic Syndrome during Carotid Artery Stenting: A Case Report.
abstract: Acute neurobehavioral deterioration during carotid artery stenting (CAS) requires prompt evaluation for serious neurological complications. We report a patient in their 70s who developed profound hyperactive delirium approximately 15 minutes after receiving prophylactic intravenous atropine (0.25 mg) during CAS. The episode was characterized by severe agitation, bilateral mydriasis, and facial flushing without focal neurological deficits. Repeated angiography and subsequent neuroimaging showed no evidence of thromboembolism, intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral edema, or cerebral hyperperfusion. Contrast-induced encephalopathy and cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome were considered but were less consistent with the overall clinical, temporal, and radiographic findings. The patient returned to neurological and cognitive baseline approximately 16 hours after symptom onset without specific antidotal treatment. The close temporal relationship to atropine exposure and characteristic neurobehavioral and autonomic features favored atropine-associated central anticholinergic syndrome, which should be considered in the differential diagnosis of acute neurobehavioral deterioration during CAS.

title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the greater omentum in a 7-year-old girl.
abstract: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is a rare neoplasm. Its preferred location is intrathoracic; there are few reports of intra-abdominal involvement, where it may affect the mesentery and retroperitoneum. A 7-year-old girl was brought in for evaluation due to fever, nonspecific lower abdominal pain, fatigue, and progressive weight loss. Laboratory tests revealed anemia, thrombocytosis, and elevated CRP. An abdominal ultrasound showed a hypoechoic mass with well-defined borders and heterogeneous content, measuring approximately 67 × 52 × 79 mm. Complete excision was performed via laparotomy. Its low incidence, varied location, nonspecific histology, and clinical heterogeneity make diagnosis extremely difficult. Only histopathology allows for a definitive diagnosis, and the cornerstone of treatment remains complete removal of the tumor. This rare condition should be included in the pediatric differential diagnosis because of its nonspecific clinical presentation, intra-abdominal mass, and high recurrence rate after incomplete resection.

title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
abstract: Introduction Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies Methods We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances ( R ² = 0.82–0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

title: CytoLens: a modular deep learning system for quantitative cervical cytology
abstract: Cervical cytology screening relies on the visual assessment of nuclear and cellular morphology across thousands of cells per slide, a labor-intensive task that could benefit from quantitative computational support. Here we present CytoLens, a modular deep learning system that detects and counts nuclei, delineates nuclei and whole cells, measures the nuclear-to-cell area ratio (N:C), classifies cells from multifocal images and scores candidate abnormality. We trained and tested each module on a public dataset matched to its task, without pooling datasets. CytoLens detected nuclei with an F1 score of 0.931 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.914–0.946) and counted 75 of 100 fields to within one nucleus. Point-prompted segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.901 for nuclei and 0.847 for whole cells and, without retraining, transferred to a second dataset in which measured N:C increased with lesion grade in parallel with expert outlines. Multifocal hierarchical classification reached a mean accuracy of 0.947 across four Bethesda-aligned categories, and abnormality scores ranked annotated abnormal candidates with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.865. These results support the evaluation of CytoLens on patient-linked clinical specimens.

title: PIEZO1 mediates mechanosensing and myofibroblastic activation of synovial fibroblasts in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
abstract: Fibrosis and inflammation of the synovium are common pathological features of joint diseases. In osteoarthritis (OA), extensive evidence supports that synovial pathology drives symptoms and disease progression, yet the mechanisms underpinning pathological synovial remodeling, including fibrosis, remain unclear. Here, we identify the mechanosensitive ion channel PIEZO1 as a critical regulator of myofibroblast-like activation of synovial fibroblasts (SFs) in post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA). Using multi-omic assessments in human and murine synovium, a murine model of joint injury, histopathology, and functional in vitro phenotyping, we demonstrate that joint injury triggers expansion of myofibroblast-like SFs concurrent with fibrotic remodeling and mechanical stiffening of the synovium. Myofibroblastic commitment of synovial progenitors was associated with activation of the YAP1 regulon, and PIEZO1 agonism drove nuclear accumulation of YAP1 in SFs. PIEZO1 was enriched in synovia of injured joints, and in cultured SFs pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation promoted αSMA enrichment and increased matrix contraction, which were both ablated by YAP1 inhibition. PIEZO1 silencing abrogated TGF-β-induced contractility and markedly altered the transcriptomic response to mechanical loading in vitro , including ECM production and neuroinflammatory programs. In vivo , acute intra-articular pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation induced a pro-fibrotic, pro-inflammatory, and anti-adipogenic transcriptomic program in synovium. Collectively, these findings establish PIEZO1 as a key mediator of the pathogenic activation of SFs and identify aberrant mechanosensing as a mechanism underlying synovial fibrosis in PTOA.

title: Self-supervised pretraining for dermoscopic lesion segmentation with limited labels: A controlled comparison of initialisation strategies
abstract: Background Self-supervised learning may improve segmentation when labelled data are limited, but its benefit may depend on model and initialisation strategy. This study evaluated in-domain masked-reconstruction pretraining across limited annotation budgets. Methods The International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2016 development set was partitioned into 765 images for self-supervised pretraining, 94 for fine-tuning and 41 for validation. Five nested annotation budgets (12–94 images) and five seeds were evaluated on the 379-image test set. A custom U-Net compared random and in-domain self-supervised initialisation; a ResNet-34 U-Net compared random, ImageNet, in-domain self-supervised and sequential ImageNet-to-self-supervised initialisation. Models trained with 94 labelled images were evaluated without adaptation on ISIC 2017. A separate experiment examined restoration-based pretraining. Results In the custom U-Net, self-supervised pretraining achieved higher mean Dice than random initialisation at all five budgets, including 0.664 versus 0.615 with 12 labels and 0.811 versus 0.768 with 94 labels. Seed-level 95% confidence intervals for paired differences excluded zero at 47 and 94 labels but not at the other budgets. With 47 labels, the self-supervised model achieved mean Dice of 0.789, compared with 0.768 for random initialisation with 94 labels. In ResNet-34, ImageNet initialisation achieved higher mean Dice than in-domain self-supervised pretraining at all five budgets, and adding self-supervised pretraining after ImageNet reduced mean Dice at four of five budgets. All six 94-label configurations achieved lower mean Dice on ISIC 2017 than ISIC 2016. In the restoration experiment, mean Dice was 0.686 with random initialisation and 0.638–0.642 following pretraining. Conclusions In-domain masked-reconstruction pretraining improved mean Dice relative to random initialisation in the custom U-Net, but not consistently in the ResNet-34 U-Net, where ImageNet initialisation performed better at every budget. Adding self-supervised pretraining after ImageNet provided no consistent gain. These findings are specific to the dermoscopic lesion-segmentation experiments and do not establish melanoma-specific diagnostic or clinical performance.

title: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen Syndrome
abstract: Clinical characteristics Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (JLNS) is characterized by bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL), vestibular dysfunction, and QTc prolongation on repeated testing. Iron deficiency anemia may be present in some people with KCNQ1 pathogenic variants. The hearing loss is most often congenital and severe to profound, although milder degrees of hearing loss have been described. Temporal bone anatomy on CT is normal. Vestibular dysfunction may result in gross motor delay (including later ages of walking), balance impairment, and absent physiologic nystagmus. In the absence of other reversible conditions that prolong the QT interval, serial 12-lead surface electrocardiograms show a prolonged QTc interval using the Bazzet formula exceeding 450 ms in prepubertal children, 460 ms in adult men, and 470 ms in adult women or a high probability long QT syndrome (LQTS) score ≥3.5. Repeated QTc prolongation must be observed, as a large overlap exists between unaffected individuals and those with LQTS. In KCNQ1-JLNS1, QTc prolongation is often severe (>500 ms) and associated with high risk for ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., torsade de pointes that can spontaneously resolve or degenerate into ventricular fibrillation), which if left untreated may result in syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD). In KCNE1-JLNS2, QTc prolongation is reported to be less severe, though significant risk for malignant ventricular arrhythmias remains. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of JLNS is established in a proband with congenital bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, electrophysiologic findings that meet diagnostic criteria for LQTS, and/or either biallelic KCNQ1 loss-of-function pathogenic variants or biallelic KCNE1 loss-of-function pathogenic variants identified by molecular genetic testing. Management Treatment of manifestations: Cochlear implantation for severe-to-profound bilateral SNHL, preferably done as soon as age six months and before age 12 months; hearing aids may be considered in those who have milder degrees of hearing loss or who are not candidates for cochlear implant; educational intervention for hearing loss; PT for gross motor delays; lifestyle modifications (avoiding QT-prolonging medication, correction and avoidance of electrolyte disturbance, and avoidance of sympathetic arousal) in those with QTc prolongation; non-selective beta-blockers (with consideration of mexiletine in those with KCNQ1-JLNS1) for long QT; left cardiac sympathetic denervation for symptomatic individuals when beta-blockers are not tolerated or are contraindicated at therapeutic doses, or for high-risk individuals; alternatively, implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) for symptomatic individuals despite beta-blocker therapy, or when beta-blockers are not tolerated or are contraindicated at therapeutic doses, and for individuals with prior cardiac arrest; standard treatment for iron deficiency anemia. Surveillance: Routine assessments per audiologist/otolaryngologist for SNHL with either a cochlear implant or amplification; assess gross motor skills every three months in infancy and every six to 12 months in childhood until PT/OT goals are met; consider annual assessment for changes in vestibular function; reassess cardiac findings including QTc monitoring and emergence of new manifestations at each visit; counsel and maintain lifestyle modifications at each visit; monitor adherence to doses and administration of prescribed medications, effectiveness and/or adverse effects of beta-blockers, and doses every three to six months during periods of rapid growth in children; evaluation of ICD at routine intervals or after ICD shock(s). Obtain complete blood count, iron studies, and gastrin levels as clinically indicated. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Perioperative precautions, including consideration of continuous heart monitoring during activation of cochlear implant; avoid drugs that prolong the QT interval; correct and avoid electrolyte abnormalities (specifically hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia); avoid sympathetic arousal triggers, such as high emotions, physical exercise, and swimming (during and while entering cold water); avoid physical activities that are known to precipitate syncopal events. Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is appropriate to evaluate all first-degree relatives of a proband with JLNS in order to identify as early as possible high-risk individuals (i.e., individuals with pathogenic variant[s] in KCNQ1 or KCNE1) who would benefit from intervention to prevent syncope, cardiac arrest, and sudden death. Assessment can include audiology examination to confirm congenital bilateral SNHL, repeated EKG assessment to establish the LQTS phenotype, and molecular genetic testing for the JLNS-related pathogenic variants identified in the proband. Perform clinical evaluation for LQTS in individuals who are heterozygotes for a KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variant. Pregnancy management: Medical therapy optimization and ICD implantation are recommended in pregnant women with LQTS who have experienced cardiac arrest, ventricular arrhythmias, and/or cardiac syncope despite beta-blocker therapy. Beta-blocker therapy should be continued in pregnant women with LQTS throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period, including during breastfeeding (i.e., until the child is weaned). Consultation with a fetal cardiologist should be performed early in pregnancy, as the fetus will have inherited one of the mother's KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variants. Fetal echocardiography is recommended to detect rhythm abnormalities, as fetal bradycardia is common in fetuses with LQTS. Genetic counseling JLNS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. At conception, each sib of an affected individual has a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being a carrier who may have long QTc only, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. When the KCNQ1 or KCNE1 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

title: Lysosomal Acid Lipase Deficiency
abstract: Clinical characteristics The phenotypic spectrum of lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (LAL-D) ranges from an infantile-onset form (previously known as Wolman disease) to childhood/adult-onset forms (previously known as cholesterol ester storage disease [CESD]). Infantile-onset LAL-D is rapidly progressive and symptoms arise within the first few days to weeks of life, with persistent vomiting, steatorrhea, and abdominal distention escalating (if untreated) to severe liver dysfunction and death within the first three to six months of life. However, with early diagnosis and initiation of treatment, long-term survival has improved significantly, although treated individuals may continue to have suboptimal growth, iron deficiency anemia, and lipid accumulation in the gastrointestinal mucosa. Those with infantile-onset disease who are treated typically experience normal long-term intellectual and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Individuals with childhood/adult-onset LAL-D typically present with otherwise unexplained transaminitis, organomegaly (splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly), and liver fibrosis that can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure. Childhood/adult-onset LAL-D does not affect long-term neurodevelopmental outcome. Affected individuals typically have hyperlipidemia, especially hypercholesterolemia. There is evidence to support efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy in stabilizing progression of liver fibrosis, reducing the need for lipid-lowering medications, and potentially lowering the risk of long-term cardiovascular complications. Diagnosis/testing The diagnosis of LAL-D is established in a proband with suggestive findings and biallelic pathogenic variants in LIPA identified by molecular genetic testing and/or deficient lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) enzyme activity in peripheral blood leukocytes or dried blood spots. Management Targeted therapies: For infantile-onset disease, enzyme replacement therapy with intravenous sebelipase alfa (premedication and desensitization protocols may be necessary) and total dietary fat restriction (total fat intake <1 g/kg/day) with supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins and essential fatty acids is recommended; some affected individuals may also benefit from hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. For childhood/adult-onset disease, intravenous administration of sebelipase alfa is recommended; dietary modification is not considered necessary, although some centers recommend dietary substrate reduction (restriction of dietary fat). Liver transplantation has been performed in individuals with adult-onset disease, especially in those with progressive liver fibrosis or cirrhosis, although there is a risk of recurrence of liver disease and it is not considered curative. Supportive care: Standard treatment for anemia/thrombocytopenia. For childhood/adult-onset disease, lipid-lowering medications for hyperlipidemia; standard treatment for cardiovascular disease, malabsorption/malnutrition, esophageal varices, and anemia/thrombocytopenia. Surveillance: For infantile-onset disease, measure weight, length/height, and mid-upper arm and abdominal circumference at each visit; assess for chronic diarrhea and monitor liver enzymes, essential fatty acids, and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) levels every six months; obtain a complete blood count every six months in children and every six to 12 months in adults to assess for anemia and thrombocytopenia; monitor anti-drug antibody (ADA) concentration for those on enzyme replacement therapy if the ALT and AST levels are >3 times the normal limit or if there are clinical concerns regarding efficacy of treatment, such as weight loss / poor weight gain, increased stool frequency, or elevated inflammatory markers (i.e., ferritin and LDH); abdominal imaging to assess the liver, spleen, and mesenteric lymph nodes and to evaluate for adrenal calcifications and hepatocellular carcinoma every six to 12 months in those with advanced cirrhosis. For childhood/adult-onset disease, measure weight and length/height in infants/children and weight in adults at each visit; consider serial abdominal circumference in adults to assess for hepatosplenomegaly; assess for chronic diarrhea and monitor essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, and K) levels with consideration of monitoring liver enzymes, chitotriosidase, ferritin, and LDH as clinically indicated; measure liver enzymes every six to 12 months or as clinically indicated based on disease severity; assess for hepatomegaly, hepatic fibrosis, and cirrhosis at every visit, as indicated by clinical/biochemical parameters; monitor anti-drug antibody (ADA) concentration as clinically indicated for those on enzyme replacement therapy; obtain a complete blood count and fasting lipid levels every six months in children and every six to 12 months (or as clinically indicated based on disease severity) in adults; upper endoscopy every three years in those with severe liver disease; abdominal imaging to assess the liver, spleen, and mesenteric lymph nodes and to evaluate for hepatocellular carcinoma as clinically indicated in those with advanced cirrhosis. Agents/circumstances to avoid: Those with thrombocytopenia should avoid use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Evaluation of relatives at risk: It is appropriate to evaluate the sibs of a proband in order to identify those who would benefit from early institution of treatment. If the LIPA pathogenic variants in the family are known, molecular genetic testing can be used to clarify the genetic status of at-risk sibs; if the LIPA pathogenic variants are not known, assay of LAL enzyme activity can be used to assist in the identification of affected sibs. Genetic counseling LAL-D is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. If both parents are known to be heterozygous for a LIPA pathogenic variant, each sib of an affected individual has at conception a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being an asymptomatic carrier, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier. If the LIPA pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

title: DeBoneDiT: Depth-Driven Conditional Bridge Diffusion Transformers for Bone Suppression in Chest X-Ray Images
abstract: Chest X-Ray (CXR) is a primary modality for diagnosing pulmonary diseases, yet the overlap of bony structures often obscures critical radiographic findings, increasing the risk of diagnostic uncertainty. While Dual-Energy Subtraction (DES) is the clinical benchmark for bone suppression, its widespread adoption is primarily hindered by specialized hardware requirements and increased radiation exposure. Recently, diffusion-based generative models have shown promise for this task, yet they are still constrained by reconstruction-biased latent compression, prior-induced domain gap, and a scarcity of high-quality paired datasets. To address these challenges, we propose DeBoneDiT, a depth-driven conditional bridge diffusion Transformer architecture for efficient high-resolution bone suppression. We first introduce Depth Auto-Encoder (DAE), a structure-aware vision tokenizer for latent compression. By incorporating a multi-level depth feature loss derived from the pretrained Depth Anything V2 encoder, DAE preserves both visual fidelity and structural consistency. Second, we formulate bone suppression as a source-conditioned Brownian bridge diffusion process, leveraging CXRs as both the diffusion prior and structural guidance to narrow the source-to-target domain gap and maintain anatomical plausibility. Furthermore, we have constructed and released SZCH-X-Rays, the largest publicly available high-quality paired dataset for bone suppression to date, comprising 741 pairs of CXR and DES soft tissue images. Extensive experiments and downstream evaluation demonstrate that DeBoneDiT achieves superior bone suppression performance with reduced computational overhead.

title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.

title: Sounds Cheesy - Bridging the Texture Gap Between Dairy and Plant-Based cheese with Non-Contact Ultrasound and AI
abstract: Plant-based cheeses often fail to reproduce the texture of dairy cheese. Closing this gap is slow because the reference methods, texture profile analysis (TPA) and sensory panels, destroy the sample and are poorly suited to screening many formulations in a timely and cost-effective manner. Here we show that non-contact, air-coupled ultrasonic imaging combined with machine learning can characterise cheese texture rapidly and without damaging the sample. Thirteen commercial products (nine dairy, four plant-based; 119 slices, 357 scans) were imaged in through-transmission at 100 kHz to give two-channel amplitude and time-of-flight C-scans, and each slice was then measured by TPA. The C-scans revealed millimetre-scale acoustic domains in ripened dairy cheeses, consistent with their fused-curd microstructure, that were absent from the homogeneous starch and oil matrix of the plant-based products. TPA showed that the texture gap is one of range and failure behaviour rather than average firmness. Mean hardness was similar for the two categories, but dairy products spanned a 7.5-fold range against 1.9-fold for plant-based products, and the plant-based products failed in a brittle, strain-softening manner rather than by ductile yielding. No single ultrasonic parameter tracked texture across products. However, a compact convolutional neural network predicted full true stress-strain loading and unloading curves from the C-scan images of unseen slices across all thirteen products without product-specific calibration. Clustering the predicted curves produced a texture map on which three plant-based slices sat with the Cheddars and one with Emmental, while soft, mozzarella-like textures remained unoccupied. The approach offers a one-minute, non-contact measurement suited to formulation screening and at-line quality control of cheese.

title: GDBA-Net: A Gated Dual-Branch Adaptation of SAM2 for Robust Cross-Domain Nuclei Segmentation
abstract: Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net

title: Continual pretraining Prostate MRI ViT Encoder for task alignment
abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

title: Contrastive uncertainty learning for robust multi-structure segmentation in lower-pelvic MR
abstract: Boundary delineation of anatomical structures in prostate MRI is often compromised by regional ambiguity. Automated segmentation methods relying on global overlap loss functions tend to be insensitive to surface deviations, leading to significant errors in ambiguous regions. Most existing uncertainty-aware methods treat uncertainty as a post-hoc quality indicator or prediction filter. We propose Contrastive Uncertainty Learning (CUL), a supervised framework that uses predictive uncertainty to directly guide representation learning. Using Monte Carlo Dropout, CUL identifies voxel-wise uncertainty and structures the embedding geometry accordingly: low-uncertainty, correctly predicted features form stable voxels while high-uncertainty or misclassified features are actively repelled, preventing feature collapse at difficult boundaries. We evaluate CUL on a 589-scan 3D prostate MRI multi-structure segmentation task (8 anatomical structures) using a ViT with UperNet decoder architecture. Average Dice ($83.38\%$) remains comparable to the baseline ($83.35\%$), while surface distance decreases significantly ($p<0.001$) across 6 of 8 anatomical structures. A hard-case analysis reveals a $22{\times}$ asymmetry between significantly improved and degraded cases ($18.8\%$ vs $0.9\%$). Ablation studies show that removing uncertainty-guided sample selection eliminates improvements for the transition zone, while replacing the contrastive objective with a boundary loss additionally removes bladder improvements, demonstrating that both uncertainty-guided sampling and the contrastive objective are essential for the observed gains. These findings demonstrate that the proposed uncertainty-guided representation learning is a useful mechanism for reducing the risk of extreme errors in safety-critical medical segmentation

title: Quantifying privacy risks in foundation model representations of brain MRI
abstract: Pretrained representations are increasingly used to share and reuse information from medical images without exposing the original scans, but it is unclear how much patient-specific information these representations retain. We investigate this question for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by evaluating five frozen pretrained encoders spanning different architectures, pretraining objectives, and training domains on two longitudinal T1-weighted datasets, OASIS-2 and MIRIAD. Under an attacker model with access to released embeddings, the corresponding public encoder, and auxiliary MRI scans, we evaluate patient linkage and sensitive-attribute inference. Across the evaluated representations, we observe substantial subject-specific information: rank-1 patient linkage reaches up to 99\% on MIRIAD and exceeds 90\% on OASIS-2 for the highest-risk representation, despite the absence of an identification objective during encoder training. We further show that the released embeddings retain information about a demographic attribute, with recorded-sex prediction reaching balanced accuracy of 90.9\% on OASIS-2 and 95.5\% on MIRIAD. Overall, our results demonstrate that replacing raw brain MRI with learned embeddings does not, by itself, eliminate patient-linkage or attribute-inference risk, and is therefore insufficient on its own to establish anonymity.

title: VascuSR: Iterative Anatomy-Aware Diffusion for CT Super-Resolution
abstract: Generative super-resolution (SR) can recover sharp detail in computed tomography (CT) images from severely downsampled observations, but the missing high-frequency content is not uniquely determined by the low-resolution input. Consequently, visually plausible reconstructions may contain anatomically unsupported vascular detail, such as missing, spurious, or incorrectly connected vessels. To overcome this challenge, we introduce VascuSR, an iterative anatomy-aware diffusion framework that combines image reconstruction with explicit 3D vascular guidance. First, to provide richer anatomical guidance, we use an explicit 3D vascular representation that captures structural information beyond individual slices. This representation also simplifies vascular refinement by allowing a lightweight 3D generative refiner to focus on vascular structure rather than complex CT appearance. Second, to guide slice-wise SR, a lightweight anatomy controller injects the refined structure into the diffusion decoder, while iterative feedback updates this guidance from each new SR volume. On re-annotated MSD Task08 and HVM datasets, VascuSR outperforms interpolation and learning-based SR baselines in segmentation accuracy (Dice and clDice) and 3D vascular structure (connectivity and mean centerline distance), while maintaining image quality comparable to its SR backbone. Compared with learning-based baselines, VascuSR reduces class-averaged connected-component counts by over 20% on both datasets and mean centerline distance by over 10% on MSD.

title: LightHybridNet: A Lightweight Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Efficient Multi-Label Ophthalmic Disease Classification in Imbalanced Fundus Images
abstract: Eye diseases are a major global cause of blindness and vision impairment, highlighting the need for accurate and early diagnosis to prevent further deterioration. Despite advances in medical imaging, classifying retinal diseases from fundus images remains challenging due to the complexity and subtlety of visual features. This study aims to develop and validate LightHybridNet, a novel lightweight hybrid deep learning framework, to improve the classification of eye diseases from fundus images. The model incorporates architectural features, such as depthwise separable convolutions and compound scaling mechanisms, to enhance diagnostic accuracy and robustness. To validate the model, the ODIR-5K dataset, comprising 8 disease categories, was used. To enhance image quality, pre-processing approaches were applied, including histogram equalisation, colour space conversion, and contrast adjustment, resulting in high-resolution images. Furthermore, image augmentation was employed to increase the dataset size, thereby improving the model's ability to generalise during training. The hybrid architecture helps the model concentrate on relevant image regions while capturing and integrating details at different scales, significantly improving classification performance. To evaluate its effectiveness, the model was compared with transfer-learning models. The results show that LightHybridNet outperforms the baselines, achieving a weighted F1-score of 91.51%, a macro AUC of 98.26%, and a Cohen's Kappa of 90.14% on the validation set. Furthermore, model interpretability was enhanced using explainable AI methods, including Grad-CAM, to identify and emphasise features influencing the decision-making process. LightHybridNet represents a promising advancement in automated ocular disease detection, offering improved diagnostic reliability for clinical use.

title: Separating mixtures of single-fiber orientation distributions for increased sensitivity to crossing white matter fibers
abstract: Intro: Diffusion MRI allows for in vivo probing of brain tissue architecture via micron-level diffusion aggregated at the millimeter scale, but crossing white matter fibers decrease the sensitivity of downstream tasks such as microstructural modeling and tractography. Current fixel-based methods for identifying the number, orientation, and spread of fibers rely on finding the peaks of fiber orientation distributions from constrained spherical deconvolution. However, this method is biased by the spreads of nearby fibers and fails at angular separations lower than approximately 40-50 degrees. Methods: In this work, we perform a constrained nonlinear optimization called fiber segmentation by signal splitting and iterative least squares estimation (FISSILE), modeling each voxel as a mixture of single-fiber distributions. We use FISSILE to fit axially symmetric fibers in simulations and on three in vivo human subjects from the Human Connectome Project, an ex vivo raccoon brain, as well as the same human subject scanned twice at two different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Results: On simulated data, FISSILE successfully identifies fibers at an angular separation of 40° and a volume fraction of 0.1 at an SNR as low as 30, while MRtrix3's fod2fixel is limited to 60° separation and 0.1 volume fraction at the same SNR. On acquired data, FISSILE identified 85.8% of white matter voxels on average in human brains and 79.4% in the raccoon with at least one fiber crossing, whereas fod2fixel identified 30.1% and 44.5%. The number of white matter fiber crossings was mildly sensitive to different noise levels in the human subject with two acquisitions. Conclusion: A method that models the crossing fiber phenomenon as an unmixing problem increases sensitivity to individual fibers for more precise characterization of anatomy.

title: Single-Pass Decision Scores Enable Rapid Classification with Adjustable Thresholds in Medical Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) answer binary clinical questions with a yes or no token, leaving the decision threshold implicit and fixed. We derive a continuous score from a single forward pass by renormalizing the probabilities of the yes and no tokens, allowing the threshold to be adapted to clinical needs without retraining. We evaluated this approach with MedGemma and Gemma-3 (4B and 27B) on six medical imaging datasets. The default threshold was frequently misaligned with the task: for identifying normal chest radiographs, MedGemma-27B labeled every image as abnormal, whereas a validation-selected threshold yielded a sensitivity of 0.945 and a specificity of 0.696. Normalization achieved the highest AUROC on four of six datasets (CheXpert: 0.819 vs. 0.777 for raw and 0.743 for text-elicited probabilities), and a single decision required 53-79 ms on one GPU. This simple post-hoc method turns medical MLLMs into fast classifiers with adjustable operating points. Code: https://github.com/TruhnLab/llm-threshold-calibration

title: DeepLNM: A Multimodal Model for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) is critical for prognostic stratification and treatment selection in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet imaging and routine pathology can yield false-negative/false-positive results. We propose DeepLNM, a multi-center foundation model for LNM prediction in CRC, evaluated with retrospective, external, prospective, and user study evidence. A multimodal dataset was assembled from three hospitals, with matched hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSI), CT scans, and text. DeepLNM achieved a mean AUC of 0.922 in the internal cohort and AUCs of 0.872 and 0.848 in two external cohorts. In a prospective cohort from a registered clinical trial (NCT07239063), DeepLNM remained robust (AUC = 0.845). In a user study, DeepLNM improved diagnostic accuracy, especially for junior pathologists (95.0%-97.3%), while reducing diagnostic time and increasing confidence. To explore the model's generalizability, it was further validated in a gastric cancer cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.793. Finally, DeepLNM identified histopathological features associated with LNM, addressing the "black-box" concern of deep learning. Together, these results position DeepLNM as a clinically preliminarily validated multimodal model for predicting LNM status in CRC, potentially facilitating the clinical translation of AI pathology.

title: Hemispheric Asymmetry of Neuroimaging Biomarkers in Early Onset Alzheimer's Disease: Clinical and Cognitive Outcomes.
abstract: Objective Individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease (AD) often exhibit amyloid, tau, and atrophy predominantly in the left or right hemisphere, but group-level analyses typically ignore inter-individual variability and changing asymmetry patterns when averaging data across participants in phenotypically diverse cohorts. Methods We examined left/right hemispheric asymmetry in amyloid positron emission tomography (PET), tau PET, and cortical atrophy in sporadic early-onset AD from 585 deeply phenotyped individuals across 2 cohorts to investigate its clinical correlates. For each imaging biomarker, we computed a global asymmetry index reflecting left/right hemisphere signal difference, and an analogous asymmetry value for PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) voxels. We examined clinical and cognitive correlates of this asymmetry across phenotypes cross-sectionally and longitudinally in a subset of 218 participants. Results Both left and right asymmetry were common for all clinical phenotypes and was correlated between imaging biomarkers. Asymmetry patterns varied spatially within phenotypes, and asymmetry in tau PET and MRI volumes was related to hemisphere-dependent cognitive deficits and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Longitudinal analyses revealed stable amyloid PET asymmetry, decreasing tau PET asymmetry, and increasing MRI volume asymmetry. Interpretation Hemispheric asymmetry is common in early onset AD and correlates with clinical outcomes. Our longitudinal findings suggest a time-lagged asymmetry peak in amyloid, then tau, then atrophy. Taken together, our results position asymmetry as an important feature of AD heterogeneity, as it provides insight into disease mechanisms and trajectories. ANN NEUROL 2026.

title: Limited sex-specific structural alterations across common epilepsies: A worldwide ENIGMA study.
abstract: Objective Epilepsy is characterized by widespread cortical and subcortical structural alterations beyond the epileptic zone. Importantly, the clinical manifestation of epilepsy, including seizure types, psychiatric comorbidities, and treatment responses, has been shown to differ between sexes. However, sex differences in structural alterations in epilepsy are seldomly reported in neuroimaging studies, partly due to limited sample sizes and single-center designs. We therefore tested whether epilepsy-related structural alterations differ between males and females, and whether the associations between structural measures and clinical characteristics vary by sex. Methods We analyzed clinician-assigned biological sex differences in common epilepsies and their related clinical variables using structural neuroimaging biomarkers in an international multicenter cohort of 1253 epilepsy patients and 1077 healthy controls. We studied cortical thickness and subcortical volume in temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and genetic generalized epilepsy (GGE). Results Both male and female patients with TLE showed widespread cortical and subcortical alterations in sex-stratified analyses, whereas GGE showed more extensive alterations in female patients and only subtle alterations in male patients. However, no significant sex-by-diagnosis interactions were identified in either the TLE (t = -2.153 to 1.705, all p FDR >.05) or GGE (t = -1.797 to 2.774, all p FDR >.05) cohort. Likewise, no significant interactions were found between sex and age at onset (t TLE = -1.835 to 1.092, t GGE = -2.394 to 1.392, all p FDR >.05) or disease duration (t TLE = -2.643 to 2.048, t GGE = -1.234 to 2.017, all p FDR >.05) in either patient group. Significance Overall, although sex differences in behavioral and clinical outcomes of epilepsy have been consistently reported in previous studies, our results indicate that sex-related clinical differences in epilepsy are not strongly captured by macroscale structural magnetic resonance imaging measures, and may instead arise from hormonal, neurochemical, or functional-network mechanisms.

title: Review of Ultrasound Diagnosis of Ichthyosis in Fetuses.
abstract: Congenital ichthyoses are inherited disorders in which the outer layer of the skin forms abnormally. Prenatal ultrasound can show a recognizable pattern in some affected fetuses, but most published evidence comes from case reports and small case series. This narrative review summarizes sonographic findings that have been reported, when they became visible, and how they should be interpreted in clinical practice. The strongest imaging literature concerns harlequin ichthyosis. Reported findings include ectropion, eclabium or persistent mouth opening, a flattened nasal contour, fixed flexion of the hands or feet, an abnormal skin surface, echogenic amniotic fluid, and polyhydramnios. However, these findings are not specific and may appear only in the second half of pregnancy. Therefore, an earlier normal scan does not exclude disease. Evidence for other congenital ichthyoses is more limited. A genotype-confirmed TGM1-related case showed facial findings similar to harlequin ichthyosis, whereas ichthyosis prematurity syndrome has a late-gestation pattern described in a small series. By contrast, X-linked ichthyosis is more often suspected from maternal serum or genetic findings than from a structural fetal ultrasound pattern. Three-dimensional ultrasound can improve display of surface anatomy when two-dimensional findings are suspicious, but its diagnostic accuracy has not been established. Fetal magnetic resonance imaging has only an adjunctive role. Overall, ultrasound is best used to recognize a phenotype, guide further assessment, and prompt genetic testing rather than to provide a stand-alone molecular diagnosis.

title: Ultrasound Features of Ossifying Renal Tumor of Infancy: A Report of Four Cases.
abstract: Ossifying renal tumor of infancy (ORTI) is an extremely rare benign renal tumor that typically presents with painless gross hematuria in infants. We describe the ultrasound features of four pathologically confirmed cases. All lesions were well-defined, hyperechoic masses located near a renal pole, protruding into the collecting system while preserving the renal contour. Calcification with posterior acoustic shadowing was present in every case. In the two cases with stored color Doppler images, internal signals were sparse. Recognition of this sonographic pattern may raise suspicion for ORTI and contribute to the preoperative differential diagnosis.

title: Accuracy of Machine Learning in Differential Diagnosis of Multiple System Atrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is frequently misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease (PD) or progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), posing significant diagnostic challenges. Objective The aim of the study was to systematically evaluate the efficacy of machine learning (ML) in differentiating MSA from other neurodegenerative disorders. Methods We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science (up to July 5, 2025), including ML-based MSA diagnostic studies. QUADAS-2 assessed bias risk, and a bivariate mixed-effects model synthesized diagnostic metrics. Results A total of 51 studies (comprising 3595 MSA patients and 18,189 total cases) were included in the systematic review. Of these, 38 studies contributed to the quantitative synthesis, whereas the remaining 13 studies were summarized qualitatively. In the primary analysis comparing MSA with PD, the pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.81-0.90), specificity 0.87 (95% CI: 0.83-0.90), and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve (AUC) 0.93 (95% CI: 0.90-0.95). Overall, pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (95% CI: 0.82-0.88), specificity 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89-0.94), and AUC 0.94 (95% CI: 0.92-0.96). Positron emission tomography (PET)-based models achieved optimal performance (sensitivity: 0.90, specificity: 0.96, AUC: 0.97), whereas deep learning models outperformed others (sensitivity: 0.93, specificity: 0.98, AUC: 0.99). Conclusion ML models integrating PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for MSA. Future work should prioritize prospective multicenter validation and standardized external testing to facilitate clinical implementation.

Results

A total of 51 studies (comprising 3595 MSA patients and 18,189 total cases) were included in the systematic review. Of these, 38 studies contributed to the quantitative synthesis, whereas the remaining 13 studies were summarized qualitatively. In the primary analysis comparing MSA with PD, the pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.81-0.90), specificity 0.87 (95% CI: 0.83-0.90), and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve (AUC) 0.93 (95% CI: 0.90-0.95). title: [Acute heart failure-management during the first 120 min : Approach for early stabilization and decongestion].
abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) is among the most common causes of emergency department, intermediate care, and intensive care unit admission and remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in contemporary therapy. The first 120 min of management are particularly critical, as this period determines not only respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization, but also trigger identification, decongestion strategy, and the foundation for subsequent prognostic improvement. This CME article provides a practical, phenotype-based approach to the early management of AHF. The proposed strategy is centered on the rapid classification of patients according to congestion ("wet" vs. "dry") and perfusion ("warm" vs. "cold") status. Stabilization and diagnostic work-up must occur simultaneously. Early assessment should focus on identifying acute coronary syndrome, clinically relevant arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism, structural heart disease, and infectious triggers. In addition to clinical examination, electrocardiography, blood gas analysis, and biomarkers, point-of-care ultrasound with lung ultrasound and focused echocardiography play a pivotal role in the first-line evaluation. From a therapeutic perspective, early noninvasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, prompt vasodilation in hypertensive presentations, and effective decongestion with intravenous loop diuretics constitute the core interventions. In cases of insufficient response, escalation strategies such as sequential nephron blockade or selective use of vasoactive agents should be considered. Structured reassessment at short intervals is essential to detect persistent congestion, evolving hypoperfusion, inadequate therapeutic response, or overlooked differential diagnoses. The article emphasizes that successful acute management must already establish the transition toward guideline-directed long-term therapy during the first hours of hospitalization, including early initiation of evidence-based heart failure medication once hemodynamic stabilization has been achieved.

title: Contralateral DTI-ALPS index as a prognostic biomarker in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma: integrating extent of resection and sex-stratified analyses.
abstract: Aim This study aimed to evaluate the independent prognostic value of the contralateral DTI-ALPS index in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, incorporating tumor morphometry, extent of resection, and sex-stratified analyses within a multivariable framework. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on 153 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from the publicly available UPENN-GBM dataset. Contralateral DTI-ALPS was calculated using DSI Studio via manual ROI placement; tumor morphometry was derived from expert-annotated segmentation labels using 3D Slicer. Survival analyses included Kaplan-Meier estimation, multivariable Cox regression, time-dependent ROC, restricted cubic spline, and sequential C-index comparison with likelihood-ratio testing. Results The contralateral DTI-ALPS index independently predicted overall survival after adjustment for age, sex, tumor volume, and GTR status (HR = 0.405, 95% CI: 0.227-0.725, p = 0.002). Each one standard deviation increase in DTI-ALPS was associated with a 24.2% reduction in mortality risk. GTR ≥ 90% (HR = 0.651, p = 0.017) and age (HR = 1.021, p = 0.007) also retained independent significance. DTI-ALPS significantly improved model discrimination beyond age alone (C-index: 0.625 → 0.653 → 0.668; likelihood-ratio test p = 0.002). Time-dependent AUC reached 0.741 at 6 months. ALPS-based stratification was more pronounced in the subtotal resection subgroup. Sex-stratified analyses showed numerically stronger associations in females, but formal interaction testing did not confirm effect modification. In an exploratory MGMT subset (n = 57), DTI-ALPS did not retain independent significance after MGMT adjustment. Conclusion The contralateral DTI-ALPS index may provide complementary prognostic information beyond established clinical predictors in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma; however, given the incomplete MGMT methylation data and ongoing methodological debate regarding the biological validity of DTI-ALPS, these findings should be considered exploratory. Prospective validation in cohorts with complete molecular and treatment data is required.

title: A rare case of bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions.
abstract: Cuboid-navicular coalitions are an exceptionally rare form of tarsal coalitions, representing less than 1% of all tarsal coalitions. Although tarsal coalitions classically become symptomatic during adolescence, cuboid-navicular coalitions may remain clinically silent until adulthood and can present with nonspecific chronic midfoot or hindfoot pain. We present a rare case of bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions in a 42-year-old man with progressive bilateral midfoot pain, associated degenerative hindfoot and midfoot changes, and bilateral peroneal tendon pathology. Initial management consisted of orthotics, bracing, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, but symptoms progressed over 8 years. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions, progressive degenerative changes, and high-grade right peroneus longus tear. The patient underwent excision of the right cuboid-navicular coalition, excision of the right lateral calcaneal tubercle with inferior peroneal retinacular release, and debridement and repair of the right peroneus longus and brevis tendons. This case highlights the importance of considering rare tarsal coalitions in adults with chronic nonspecific midfoot pain and emphasizes the value of MRI and CT for diagnosis, characterization of associated pathology, and operative planning.
